config.title: Binary Search

intro.title: Binary Search
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that implements the binary search algorithm to efficiently find a target value in a sorted array. You will learn the core concept of divide-and-conquer, where the search space is repeatedly halved by comparing the target to the middle element. The main constructs involved are arrays, while loops, and conditional logic to manage indices and comparisons. By the end, you will understand how binary search achieves O(log n) time complexity, making it much faster than linear search for large datasets.
intro.usecase: Binary search is essential for efficiently finding items in sorted datasets, a common requirement in modern applications. You'll use it when implementing autocomplete suggestions in search bars, filtering large product catalogs in e-commerce sites, or navigating sorted user lists in admin dashboards. As a developer, you might apply binary search to optimize performance when handling sorted arrays of timestamps in analytics tools or implementing pagination with sorted results. This algorithm ensures your applications remain responsive even when processing thousands of items.

objectives: Implement a binary search function that accepts a sorted array and a target value.
Initialize and manipulate pointers to track the search range within the array.
Construct a loop that repeatedly halves the search space until the target is found or the range is exhausted.
Apply conditional logic to compare the middle element with the target and adjust pointers accordingly.
Configure the function to return the index of the target if found, or a sentinel value like -1 if not present.
Integrate the binary search function into a simple test script to verify its correctness with sample data.
Control the search process by ensuring the loop terminates correctly for all possible inputs.

content.body: Imagine you're looking for a word in a dictionary. You wouldn't start at page 1 and read every word, would you? You'd open to the middle and eliminate half the book at a time. That's binary search! Today we'll implement this clever algorithm in JavaScript.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain why binary search requires sorted data
2. Implement binary search to find a target value
3. Handle cases where the target isn't found
4. Visualize how the search space gets cut in half each step
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's play a guessing game. I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100. You can only ask "is it greater than X?" or "is it less than X?" questions. What's your first question to eliminate the most possibilities?
content.title: Try it

content.body: If you ask "is it greater than 50?" and I say "no," you've eliminated numbers 51-100. Now you have 1-50 left. What's your next question to again eliminate half of what remains?
content.title: Think deeper

content.body: You instinctively went to the middle each time! By asking about the midpoint, you eliminated half the possibilities with each question. This is much faster than asking "is it 1?" "is it 2?" and so on.
content.title: What you did

content.body: Now imagine searching through 1 million sorted numbers. Checking each one would take forever. But if we cut the search space in half each time, we'd find any number in at most 20 steps! Can you see how? Click Show me on the next step for a visual walkthrough.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Binary search works because the data is sorted. This ordering lets us make a crucial decision at each step: if our target is less than the middle element, it must be in the left half; if greater, it must be in the right half. We can safely ignore the other half entirely.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Repeatedly cut the range in half; only one half can contain the answer.

content.body: Here's the binary search algorithm: Start with the whole array. Find the middle element. Compare it to your target. If they match, you're done! If target is smaller, search the left half. If target is larger, search the right half. Repeat until found or the search space is empty.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Searching for 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]:
1. Middle is 16 (index 4). 23 > 16 → search right half [23, 38, 56, 72, 91]
2. Middle is 56 (index 7). 23 < 56 → search left half [23, 38]
3. Middle is 23 (index 5). Found!

content.body:
1. Set left pointer to start (0) and right pointer to end (array.length - 1)
2. While left <= right:
   a. Calculate middle index
   b. If array[middle] equals target, return middle
   c. If target < array[middle], move right to middle - 1
   d. If target > array[middle], move left to middle + 1
3. If loop ends, target not found (return -1)
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called binarySearch that takes a sorted array and a target value. Return -1 for now.
steps.hint: Remember function syntax: function name(parameters) { return value; }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function skeleton.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure your function takes two parameters: arr and target.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need: function binarySearch(arr, target) { return -1; }

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create left and right variables to track the search range. Set left to 0 and right to arr.length - 1.
steps.hint: Remember array indices start at 0, so the last index is length - 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we have boundaries for our search.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Check that right is arr.length - 1, not arr.length.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need: let left = 0; let right = arr.length - 1;

steps.title: Create the search loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues as long as left <= right. This means there's still a valid search range.
steps.hint: The loop should run while the left pointer hasn't passed the right pointer.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The loop will keep searching while there's range to check.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure it's while (left <= right) with the less-than-or-equal operator.

steps.title: Calculate the middle
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, calculate the middle index. Use Math.floor((left + right) / 2) to avoid decimals.
steps.hint: Math.floor() rounds down to the nearest whole number.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Now we can check the middle element each iteration.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Remember Math.floor to get a whole number index.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need: let mid = Math.floor((left + right) / 2);

steps.title: Compare and adjust pointers
steps.instruction: Add the core logic: if arr[mid] equals target, return mid. If target is less, move right to mid - 1. If target is greater, move left to mid + 1.
steps.hint: Remember: when target is smaller, we search left; when larger, we search right.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! This is the complete binary search logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there! Check all three cases: equal, less than, and greater than.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need: if equal return mid; else if target < arr[mid] adjust right; else adjust left.

steps.title: Test your implementation
steps.instruction: Call your function with a sorted array and target. Use console.log to see the result. Try finding 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91].
steps.hint: Remember arrays are zero-indexed, so 23 should be at index 5.
steps.feedbackCorrect: 🎉 Excellent! Your binary search is working perfectly!
steps.feedbackPartial: Good! Now add the test call: console.log(binarySearch([2,5,8,12,16,23,38,56,72,91], 23));

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented binary search. Remember:
• Binary search only works on sorted arrays (this lets us eliminate half each time)
• Each comparison cuts the search space in half
• The -1 return handles the "not found" case
• This algorithm runs in O(log n) time – incredibly efficient for large datasets!

Try testing with targets that aren't in the array to see it return -1.
